findings.location: Results, para 1 (race/ethnicity of mothers interviewed at child age 18 y)
findings.quote: One mother (0.2%) reported Hispanic ethnicity, and 617 mothers (98.8%) reported non-Hispanic ethnicity.
findings.reproduction_problem: grim_percentage is MCP-only and has no CLI verb; the grim-sweep command given reproduces the identical conclusion (n=618 is not viable for 98.8%). See finding nonhispanic_pct_grim_sweep for the natively runnable form.
findings.notes: n=618 is a STATED denominator, not an assumed one: the paper says 618 mothers were interviewed at child age 18 y, the arm split 192+426=618 reconciles exactly, and the three race counts 5+578+35 sum to exactly 618. No integer count out of 618 yields 98.8%. The printed count 617 gives 617/618 = 99.8%, which IS attainable. This is therefore an isolated typographical error (99.8 mis-set as 98.8), not a data-integrity problem: the companion percentages 0.8/93.5/5.7 all pass GRIM at n=618. Flagged `impossible` because the printed value violates arithmetic as written, but the benign explanation is strongly supported.

findings.location: Results, Intergenerational Mobility, para 1
findings.quote: in the control group, having a mother with severe hypertension was associated with a higher chance (11.3 correlation coefficient) of having a female child with severe hypertension. This association was absent in the treated group, with a significant 0.188 treatment difference in the intergenerational correlation coefficients.

computed.ratio_to_companion_value: 11.3 vs 0.188 -- differ by a factor of ~60

findings.reproduction: No validated tool applies; verified by reading the printed sentence against the definition of a correlation coefficient.
findings.notes: A correlation coefficient of 11.3 is definitionally impossible. The companion figure in the same sentence -- a 0.188 treatment difference in the SAME intergenerational correlation coefficients -- is internally inconsistent with 11.3 by a factor of ~60, but is fully consistent with a control-group correlation of 0.113. The overwhelmingly likely explanation is a decimal/typesetting error (0.113 printed as 11.3), not a data problem. Recorded as impossible-as-printed; the substantive point is that the number as published cannot be interpreted and the underlying analysis lives in eTable 8 of an unavailable supplement.

findings.location: Table 1 (all four significant female ARRs) and Abstract

computed.tool_note: the interval behaves like a 99% CI, not the stated 95% -- check the reported level

findings.notes: Produced by check_estimate_ci (CLI verb: check-ci); technique recorded as `reconcile` because the schema enum has no check_estimate_ci entry. All FOUR of Table 1's significant female effects -- the paper's headline offspring findings, repeated verbatim in the Abstract -- reconcile with their printed p-values only if the intervals are 99%, not the labelled 95%. Read as genuine 95% intervals, the recovered p-values are 0.008, 0.016, 0.033 and 0.018 against printed .002, .003, .007 and <.001, i.e. 4-18x larger. Either the intervals are mislabelled or the p-values do not correspond to them. The tool returned `consistent` per-row because it found an alternative confidence level that reconciles each; the finding is the CONTRADICTION with the printed '95% CI' label, which the tool cannot see. The p<.001 case is the most consequential: a 95% interval of (0.046, 0.748) implies p ~ 0.018, nowhere near the claimed threshold. Tables 2-4 do NOT show this signature, so it is localised to Table 1.

findings.location: Tables 1-4 and Results text, ARR (95% CI) with P value columns

computed.direction_of_error: bidirectional -- recovered p is sometimes larger (0.881, 0.784, 0.698, 0.815, 0.605, 0.663) and sometimes smaller (1.454) than printed

findings.notes: Produced by check_estimate_ci (CLI verb: check-ci). Across the ARR rows the printed p-values do not reproduce from the printed intervals, and the discrepancies run in BOTH directions. Bidirectionality argues against a single systematic transcription error and is consistent with the p-values being generated on a different scale or from a different model than the intervals -- e.g. p from the underlying logistic (odds-ratio) coefficient while the CI is a delta-method-transformed relative risk. That would be a legitimate computation but an internally inconsistent presentation, since a reader cannot recover either quantity from the other. Contrast the difference-scale estimates (finding lsmd_estimates_consistent), which reconcile cleanly.

findings.quote: Severe obesity at age 12 and 18 y | Female | 0.12 (0.33) | 0.02 (0.16) ... Stage 2 hypertension at age 12 and 18 y | Mothers of females | 0.27 (0.44) | 0.05 (0.23)

reported.per_arm_n: NOT REPORTED anywhere in the paper

findings.reproduction: metascience debit --mean 0.31 --sd 0.47 --n 207 --data-type binary && metascience debit --mean 0.31 --sd 0.47 --n 212 --data-type binary
findings.notes: IMPORTANT NEGATIVE RESULT. DEBIT is the natural check here -- every outcome is a 0/1 indicator whose SD is fully determined by its mean and n -- but the paper never reports per-arm sample sizes, only a combined row N. An initial batch run using arm sizes inferred from the 228:514 allocation returned 3 'impossible' rows. Every one of those three REVERSES to consistent at a different plausible n: 0.31 (0.47) is impossible at n=212 but consistent at n=207 and n=400; 0.02 (0.16) is consistent at n=80 and n=120; 0.05 (0.23) is consistent at n=110. The three flags were artefacts of my own assumed denominators, not properties of the data, and are withdrawn. Per rulebook rule 4 no DEBIT verdict on this paper can rise above indeterminate. A second caveat compounds this: the paper does not state whether these proportions are raw sample means or lasso/IPW-adjusted, and if adjusted the SD is not pinned by the mean at all. 19 of 23 rows were consistent at the inferred n, so there is no evidence of a problem -- only an inability to test.

findings.notes: Produced by check_estimate_ci (CLI verb: check-ci). The maternal hypertension headline results -- the paper's other principal claim -- pass. Each estimate sits at its log-CI midpoint and the intervals behave as genuine 95% intervals (inferred_confidence_level null, unlike Table 1). Recovered p's run 1-4x the printed values, which the tool accepts at the printed precision; the two '<.001' rows recover 0.0024 and 0.0011, so the claimed threshold is not quite met on the interval alone but is within rounding tolerance. Male severe obesity at 12 and 18 y
Mothers of males stage 2 HTN at 12 and 18 y

reported.verbal_claim: no intervention effect / no effect / no differences were significant

computed.verdict: equivalence cannot be assessed; no conclusion of 'no effect' is licensed by these numbers alone

findings.notes: Produced by absence_of_evidence (CLI verb: absence-of-evidence); technique recorded as `manual` because the schema enum has no absence_of_evidence entry. The paper's null claims are stated flatly ('no effect', 'No intervention effect was found') in the Abstract, Key Points and Conclusions, but the underlying intervals are wide enough to be compatible with substantial effects -- up to a 6.4-fold difference for female offspring stage 1 hypertension and a 2.2-fold INCREASE for male offspring obesity. The male-obesity interval (0.963-2.197) is in fact directionally adverse and borderline. Because the paper states no smallest effect size of interest, the tool correctly declines to judge equivalence, and that refusal is the recorded result. The asymmetry matters editorially: the same evidential standard is not applied to the positive female findings and the null male findings.

findings.location: Table 1, Severe obesity at age 12 and 18 y, Female; Abstract
findings.quote: the risk of severe obesity by 81% (ARR, 0.185; 95%CI, 0.046-0.748; P < .001)
findings.notes: Produced by check_effect_plausibility (CLI verb: effect-size). Guards against a false positive. An 81% relative risk reduction sounds extraordinary, but on the standardised scale it is d = 0.35, squarely at the medicine_rct median of 0.3 -- because a large RELATIVE reduction on a rare binary outcome (12% vs 2%) is a modest ABSOLUTE and standardised effect. The headline effect magnitude is therefore NOT implausible and should not be flagged as too-good-to-be-true. Caveat: per-arm ns were inferred from the 228:514 allocation, though d is nearly insensitive to them; and d benchmarks are calibrated on continuous outcomes, so this is an approximate comparison.

unchecked.location: eTable 2 in Supplement 2 -- Balancing Tests, Baseline Covariates
unchecked.reason: MOST SIGNIFICANT GAP. The baseline balance table is the primary randomization-integrity check and would be the natural target for csf_test and bayesian_table1_dispersion (Carlisle/Fujii baseline-similarity analysis). Supplement 2 was not provided, so no baseline p-values or group means/SDs were available and neither tool could be run. The paper asserts only that 'The balancing tests showed few baseline differences' -- an unquantified claim. Note this matters more than usual here: the authors used post-double-selection lasso specifically to correct baseline imbalances, so the extent of those imbalances is load-bearing for every estimate in the paper.

unchecked.location: eTable 3 in Supplement 2 -- Ex-Post Power Calculations
unchecked.reason: verify_power_analysis requires the effect size, alpha, target power and n actually used; the paper states only 'at least 80% power (alpha = .05) for the majority of outcomes' without naming the effect size assumed or which outcomes qualify. Inputs are in the unavailable supplement, so the calculation cannot be reproduced. Separately worth flagging editorially: these are EX-POST (post hoc) power calculations, computed from observed effects, which are widely regarded as uninformative about a completed study.

Supplement 2 not provided. This withholds the inverse-probability-weighting robustness analysis (eTable 9), the unbalanced-covariate robustness check (eTable 10), the self-report-exclusion robustness checks (eTables 11-12), the mediation analysis (eTable 7) and the intergenerational correlation analysis (eTable 8) -- the last being the source of the impossible 11.3 correlation coefficient, which therefore cannot be diagnosed further.

unchecked.location: Figure (quantile regression treatment effects, panels A-F)
unchecked.reason: Vector-drawn quantile-regression plots with 90% CI bands and no numeric values in the caption or body. No coefficients, standard errors or deciles are reported anywhere in text, so nothing was digitizable to a checkable statistic. Any values read off the marks would be tier-2 figure_pixels provenance and barred from the exact-arithmetic tools in any case.

Reported as bare point estimates with no standard errors, confidence intervals, p-values or component coefficients. Gelbach decomposition inputs are in eTable 7 (unavailable). No validated tool can test a proportion-mediated figure without its variance components.

unchecked.location: Per-arm sample sizes for every cell of Tables 1-4
unchecked.reason: Never reported -- only a combined row N. This is what defeated DEBIT (see finding debit_binary_proportions_indeterminate) and it also blocks recalc_independent_t, recalc_chi_squared and reconstruct_2x2 on the group proportions, since no cell counts can be recovered. The single most consequential reporting omission for verifiability in this paper.

unchecked.location: Maternal age at randomization, mean (SD) 18.1 (3.2), n=742
unchecked.reason: GRIM and GRIMMER were deliberately NOT run. Age in years is a continuous measure and the paper does not state it was recorded as whole years; applying integer-scale tools to a continuous variable is the most common route to a false accusation. Even had it been integer-valued, GRIM granularity at n=742 (1/742 = 0.0013) is far finer than the reported 1 decimal place, so the test would be vacuous.

unchecked.location: Romano-Wolf multiple-hypothesis-testing p-values (69 MHT values across Tables 1-4)
unchecked.reason: No validated tool reproduces a bootstrap stepdown correction. The MHT column was compared against the uncorrected p column by direct inspection only (see finding mht_p_smaller_than_uncorrected_p); the corrected values themselves could not be recalculated without the 1000-replication bootstrap and the underlying data.

unchecked.location: Multiplicity across the full analysis (69 ARR tests in main tables plus supplementary outcomes)
unchecked.reason: Recorded as an anatomy fact rather than a tool finding: the Romano-Wolf correction was applied WITHIN 6 blocks of 3 outcomes per table, i.e. within-table only, not across the 4 tables or across the sex strata jointly. No tool in the suite evaluates whether a stated correction's blocking structure is adequate for the full family of tests, so this is flagged for editorial judgment. Relevant context: the paper states these outcomes were not primary or secondary in the original protocol and that sex was not hypothesized as a moderator.

studies.label: Nurse-Family Partnership Memphis RCT, 18-year follow-up (offspring ages 12 and 18 y)

hypotheses.statement: Prenatal and infancy nurse home visitation reduces offspring obesity and severe obesity at ages 12 and 18 years, with the effect concentrated in female offspring.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: This study examines the Memphis program's effects on maternal and offspring obesity and hypertension at offspring ages 12 and 18 years, aspects of health that were not primary or secondary outcomes in the original study design or the follow-ups at child ages 12 and 18 years.

hypotheses.statement: Prenatal and infancy nurse home visitation reduces maternal stage 1 and stage 2 hypertension at child ages 12 and 18 years, with the effect concentrated in mothers of female offspring.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: given that obesity and hypertension were not included as primary or secondary outcomes in the original protocol and numerous outcomes were analyzed, we accounted for multiplicity of tests within outcome categories

hypotheses.statement: Offspring sex moderates the intervention effect on obesity and hypertension.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: First, given that sex was not hypothesized as a moderator of NFP effects in the original study protocol, we examined NFP-control differences for a variety of baseline covariates.

hypotheses.statement: Health improvements at child age 12 years mediate sustained treatment effects at child age 18 years, and NFP breaks intergenerational persistence in hypertension.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: We also found that health improvements at child age 12 years were significant mediators of the sustained treatment effects at child age 18 years.

variables.name: Stage 1 hypertension (maternal: SBP >= 130 mm Hg or DBP >= 80 mm Hg)

variables.name: Stage 2 hypertension (maternal: SBP >= 140 mm Hg or DBP >= 90 mm Hg)

variables.name: Length of gestation

variables.name: Birth weight

variables.name: Preterm birth

variables.name: Any maternal health condition at child age 18 y (self-reported)

variables.name: Count of maternal health conditions at offspring age 18 y
